templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and earn {rate|money0} per hour. This week you worked {hours|int} hours. Your pay stub shows two deductions: {pct|pct} of your gross pay for taxes, and a flat {flat|money0} for health insurance. These amounts are only an example.
templates.prompt: What is your take-home pay for the week?

options.text: Your take-home pay is {net|money} for the week.
options.why: Gross pay is {rate|money0} times {hours|int} hours, or {gross|money}. Taxes take {pct|pct} of that, or {tax|money}, and the flat {flat|money0} comes out as well, leaving {net|money}.

options.text: Your take-home pay is {wrongNoFlat|money} for the week.
options.why: This figure subtracts only the percentage for taxes. The flat {flat|money0} insurance charge also comes out of gross pay.
options.misconception: I only need to subtract the percentage deduction.

options.text: Your take-home pay is {wrongNoTax|money} for the week.
options.why: This figure subtracts only the flat insurance charge. The {pct|pct} tax deduction, which is {tax|money} of {gross|money}, also comes out.
options.misconception: A flat charge is the only real deduction.

options.text: Your take-home pay is {wrongPctAsDollars|money} for the week.
options.why: This treats {pct|pct} as if it were {pct|int} dollars. A percentage deduction is a share of gross pay, which here is {tax|money}.
options.misconception: A percentage deduction can be subtracted like a dollar amount.

templates.principle: To find take-home pay, start with gross pay, take a percentage deduction as a share of gross pay, and subtract flat deductions as dollar amounts.

review.notes: Hypothetical deductions, explicitly labeled as an example; no claim about real tax rates or rules. Distractors correspond to three common calculation errors.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You are preparing {k|int} packages, and each package needs {n|int} labels. Labels are sold only in packs of {p|int}, and you are ordering the smallest number of packs that covers the need.
templates.prompt: How many packs should you order?

options.text: You need to order {packsCeil|int} packs of labels.
options.why: The total need is {k|int} times {n|int}, or {total|int} labels. Packs hold {p|int} each, and a partly needed pack must still be bought, so round up to {packsCeil|int}.

options.text: You need to order {packsFloor|int} packs of labels.
options.why: Rounding down leaves you short. {total|int} labels are needed, and {packsFloor|int} packs only hold {floorLabels|int}.
options.misconception: I can round down when the remainder is small.

options.text: You need to order {packsNoMultiply|int} packs of labels.
options.why: This only counts one label per package. Each package needs {n|int} labels, so multiply before dividing into packs.
options.misconception: I only need to count the packages.

options.text: You need to order {packsExtra|int} packs of labels.
options.why: This buys more than needed. You were asked for the smallest number of packs, and {packsCeil|int} already covers the need.

templates.principle: To estimate supplies, find the total need first, divide by the pack size, and round up to whole packs.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Client|a}'s order comes to {price|money0} before any discount. A {pct|pct} discount applies to the whole order. This discount is only an example.
templates.prompt: What is the amount due after the discount?

options.why: A {pct|pct} discount on {price|money0} is {off|money}. Subtracting that from {price|money0} leaves {due|money}.
This subtracts {pct|int} dollars instead of {pct|pct} of the price. A percent discount is a share of the total.
options.misconception: A percent discount works like a dollar amount.

options.why: This is the size of the discount, not the amount left to pay. The discount still has to be subtracted from {price|money0}.
options.misconception: The discount amount is the amount due.

options.why: This adds the percentage instead of subtracting it. A discount lowers the price.

templates.principle: To apply a percent discount, find that percent of the price and subtract it from the price.

review.notes: Discount is explicitly an example; no claim about real policies.

templates.scenario: You are checking this expense report at {workplace|the} before it goes to your supervisor.
templates.prompt: Tap the line with the problem.

segments.whyFine: The mileage cost matches miles times the rate.
This line is a single amount with nothing to check.
This line is a single amount with nothing to check.

segments.why: The items add up to {total|money}, not {wrongTotal|money}, so the total is wrong.

templates.principle: Check that a total equals the sum of its parts before submitting a report.

templates.scenario: You keep your own record of hours worked at {workplace|the}. For the pay period, your record shows {logged|int} hours, but your pay stub shows {stub|int} hours.

options.text: Compare your record with the stub, note the {diff|int}-hour difference, and take both to payroll.
options.why: Checking your own record against the stub shows exactly where the difference is, and bringing both to payroll lets them find and fix the cause.

options.text: Wait for the next paycheck and see whether the missing {diff|int} hours are added automatically.
options.why: A missing entry will not necessarily fix itself. Raising it now makes a correction more likely.

options.text: Add {diff|int} extra hours to your next timesheet so that the totals even out over time.
options.why: Recording hours you did not work is inaccurate and can cause bigger problems. The original difference needs to be corrected properly.
options.misconception: I can balance the difference myself later.

options.text: Tell payroll you were underpaid and ask for the full amount right away, without showing your record.
options.why: Without your record, payroll has nothing to check. Bringing evidence makes your case clear and quicker to settle.
options.misconception: Making a firm demand is more effective than showing proof.

templates.principle: When numbers do not match, compare your own record to the document, find the difference, and bring both to the person who can fix it.

review.notes: Hypothetical hours; no claims about payroll law.

templates.timing: Verification comes before asking for a correction.

templates.scenario: You are estimating the cost of supplies for a project at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Find the price of one item
Multiply it by the number of items needed
Add the totals for all the different items
Compare the final total with the budget

precedence.why: You need the unit price before you can multiply.
Each item's total must be known before you add them together.
You compare the budget with the final total, not with a partial one.

templates.principle: Estimate costs by finding unit prices, multiplying by quantities, adding totals, and then comparing with the budget.
